Short questions to check your understanding of the lecture *Organelles compared: keeping the cell in balance*. Try each on paper first, then open the hint or the answer. The tag after each question shows the learning outcome (ELO) it practises.

---

**Q1.** The nucleus is surrounded by two membranes. Why do the pH and free Ca²⁺ in the nucleoplasm still follow those of the cytosol? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do the nuclear pores let through without a signal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Nuclear pores** are large open channels. Ions and small molecules (below about 40 kDa) pass through them freely by diffusion, so H⁺ and Ca²⁺ equilibrate between the cytosol and the nucleoplasm. Only large molecules need a signal and transport receptors. The nucleus is therefore a separate compartment for proteins and RNA, but not for ions.
:::

---

**Q2.** What is the nuclear lamina made of, where is it, and name two of its jobs. `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
It is a type of intermediate filament.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A mesh of **lamins** (A-type and B-type), which are intermediate-filament proteins, lying just **under the inner nuclear membrane**. Jobs: gives the nucleus its **shape and mechanical strength**; **anchors chromatin** (often silent heterochromatin) at the edge; links through the envelope to the cytoskeleton; it is taken apart by **phosphorylation** in mitosis so the envelope can break down.
:::

---

**Q3.** Peroxisomes make hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), which is toxic. Why is this not a problem for the cell, and why does it make sense to do these reactions in a separate organelle? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which enzyme is packed into the same organelle?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The oxidases that make H₂O₂ sit in the same small compartment as **catalase**, which immediately breaks H₂O₂ down to water and oxygen (2 H₂O₂ → 2 H₂O + O₂). Keeping production and destruction together means H₂O₂ hardly reaches the rest of the cell, where it would damage proteins, lipids and DNA. It is the same logic as keeping acid hydrolases in lysosomes: dangerous chemistry stays in one box.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does a lipid droplet have only **one** layer of phospholipids around it, while other organelles have a bilayer? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where are the neutral fats deposited when a droplet forms, and what is inside the droplet?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Neutral fats (triglycerides, cholesterol esters) are made in the ER and collect **between the two leaflets** of the ER membrane. The lens of fat buds towards the cytosol, taking only the **cytosolic leaflet** with it. The inside of the droplet is oil, not water, so a single layer is enough: the fatty tails of the phospholipids face the oil, and the heads face the cytosol.
:::

---

**Q5.** What is an organelle contact site? Give one example and say what passes there. `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far apart are the membranes, and do they fuse?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A place where the membranes of two organelles are held **10–30 nm apart by tether proteins, without fusing**, so each keeps its own lumen. Examples: **ER–mitochondria**: Ca²⁺ released by IP₃ receptors in the ER is taken up by mitochondria (which speeds up the citric acid cycle), and lipids such as phosphatidylserine move from the ER to mitochondria. **ER–plasma membrane**: STIM in the ER opens ORAI in the plasma membrane when the ER Ca²⁺ store is empty (store-operated Ca²⁺ entry).
:::

---

**Q6.** Put these compartments in order from the most acidic to the most alkaline: cytosol, lysosome, mitochondrial matrix, early endosome, trans-Golgi. `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One of them is above pH 7.2.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
**Lysosome** (4.5–5) < **trans-Golgi** (≈ 6.0) ≈ **early endosome** (6.0–6.5) < **cytosol** (7.2) < **mitochondrial matrix** (≈ 8). The trans-Golgi and early endosome overlap; either order between them is fine. The lumen compartments are acidified by the V-type H⁺ pump; the matrix is alkaline because the electron transport chain pumps H⁺ out of it.
:::

**Q7.** A drug blocks the SERCA pump. What happens to free Ca²⁺ in (a) the ER and (b) the cytosol, and (c) why does the cell then switch on the unfolded protein response? `[ELO 5]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ from the cytosol into the ER. The ER leaks Ca²⁺ all the time. Which ER chaperones bind Ca²⁺?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) The ER **empties**: Ca²⁺ keeps leaking out but is no longer pumped back. (b) Cytosolic Ca²⁺ **rises** for a while (until pumps in the plasma membrane remove it), and the empty store activates STIM–ORAI entry. (c) Ca²⁺-binding chaperones such as **calnexin and calreticulin** need ER Ca²⁺ to fold proteins. Without it, unfolded proteins pile up, and the sensors IRE1, PERK and ATF6 start the **unfolded protein response**. (Thapsigargin is such a drug, used in experiments.)
:::

**Q8.** Name the gene or protein that is defective, and the organelle affected, in (a) Hutchinson–Gilford progeria and (b) Zellweger syndrome. How does lonafarnib help in (a)? `[ELO 5]` `[ELO 9]`

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
One disease keeps a lipid anchor that should be cut off; the other cannot import enzymes.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) **Lamin A** (LMNA gene) → **nuclear lamina**. A splice mutation removes 50 amino acids including the cleavage site, so **progerin** keeps its **farnesyl** lipid, stays stuck on the inner nuclear membrane and distorts the nucleus. **Lonafarnib** inhibits **farnesyltransferase**, so less progerin carries the lipid anchor; nuclei look more normal and survival improves. (b) A **PEX** gene (import machinery) → **peroxisomes**. Enzymes cannot be imported, peroxisomes are empty "ghosts", very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate and plasmalogens are missing.
:::
